items.q: What is the indication for antibiotics in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
opts: A low serum C3 at presentation
items.exp: Antibiotics in PSGN are indicated for an active sore throat; they do not alter the course of the established glomerulonephritis. (Book p777)

items.q: Match the antibiotic regimen for an active sore throat — 1) Benzathine penicillin  2) Oral penicillin V  3) Penicillin allergy … A) 500 mg BD for 5–10 days  B) Erythromycin  C) Single dose of 1.2 million units
items.exp: Regimens: single-dose benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units; oral penicillin V 500 mg BD × 5–10 days; erythromycin when penicillin-allergic. (Book p777)

items.q: The single dose of benzathine penicillin used for an active sore throat in PSGN is:
items.exp: Single-dose benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units is one of the listed options for an active sore throat. (Book p777)

items.q: Oral penicillin V for an active sore throat in PSGN is given as 500 mg twice daily for:
items.exp: Oral penicillin V: 500 mg BD × 5–10 days, as an alternative to single-dose benzathine penicillin. (Book p777)

items.q: Fill up: In penicillin allergy with an active sore throat, the antibiotic listed is ______.
items.exp: In penicillin allergy, erythromycin is the listed antibiotic for an active sore throat. (Book p777)

items.q: The note on this page states that nephrotic syndrome shows no pulmonary oedema.
opts: True — pulmonary oedema is a feature of the nephritic, not the nephrotic, picture
False — pulmonary oedema is the rule in nephrotic syndrome
True, but only in children under 5 years
False — the note is about PIGN, not nephrotic syndrome
items.exp: Note: 'Nephrotic syndrome: no pulmonary oedema' — contrasting the intravascular-volume depletion of nephrotic syndrome with the volume overload of the nephritic syndrome. (Book p777)

items.q: With prompt treatment, what percentage of PSGN patients recover in 3–5 days?
items.exp: Recovery: 99% recover in 3–5 days with prompt treatment. (Book p777)

items.q: Six months after an episode of PSGN, a boy still has 5–10 RBCs/hpf on urine microscopy but normal BP, creatinine and serum C3. What is the correct advice?
opts: Persistent microhaematuria can follow PSGN and has no significance
Immediate repeat renal biopsy for recurrent disease
Long-term steroid therapy to clear the haematuria
This proves incomplete recovery with impending CKD
items.exp: Recovery point 2: microhaematuria can persist after treatment and has no significance — unlike the persistent ↓C3 (>8 weeks) that would warrant biopsy. (Book p777)

items.q: A 6-year-old treated for PSGN is reviewed at 8 weeks: haematuria persists but serum C3 has normalised. The correct interpretation is:
opts: Persistent microhaematuria after PSGN has no significance, whereas a C3 still low beyond 8 weeks would suggest C3 GN and warrant biopsy
Both findings indicate a recurrence of PSGN, which requires a second course of penicillin
The persistent haematuria indicates progression to CKD, and C3 must be rechecked monthly for one year
A normal C3 at 8 weeks excludes PSGN, so the original diagnosis must be revised
items.exp: Recovery point: 99% recover in 3-5 days with prompt treatment, and microhaematuria may persist after treatment with no significance; follow-up is by serum C3, normally normal by 8 weeks, and persistence beyond that points to C3 GN and biopsy. PSGN also does not recur. (Book p777)

items.q: Follow-up after an episode of PSGN is done with:
items.exp: Follow-up: serum C3, expected to be normal after 8 weeks; persistence beyond 8 weeks suggests C3 GN and needs biopsy. (Book p777)
